What is Sentry and why use it instead of just logs?

Sentry is an error and performance monitoring platform. Instead of searching raw logs, it captures exceptions with full stack traces, request/user context and breadcrumbs, deduplicates them into issues, shows frequency and affected users, links them to releases and commits, and alerts the team. Logs are still needed for general event history; Sentry makes errors actionable.
What is a DSN? Is it safe to expose it in a front-end app?

The DSN is the project-specific endpoint and public key the SDK uses to send events. It only permits submitting events, not reading data, so it is acceptable in browser bundles – Sentry's own guidance treats it as public for client SDKs. Abuse (spam events) is mitigated with allowed domains, rate limits and inbound filters. Still keep it in environment config, not hard-coded.
How do you integrate Sentry with Spring Boot?

Add sentry-spring-boot-starter-jakarta (Spring Boot 3) and set sentry.dsn, environment, release and traces-sample-rate. It auto-captures unhandled exceptions from controllers, adds request data, and with the Logback integration turns ERROR logs into events and lower levels into breadcrumbs. Exceptions handled by your own @ControllerAdvice may need an explicit Sentry.captureException if you still want them reported.
How do you integrate Sentry with Angular?

Install @sentry/angular, call Sentry.init() in main.ts before bootstrapping, and provide Sentry.createErrorHandler() as Angular's ErrorHandler. Add browserTracingIntegration() and TraceService for route-change performance, and set tracePropagationTargets so trace headers flow to your API for distributed tracing. Upload source maps in CI so stack traces map back to TypeScript.
What are breadcrumbs?

Breadcrumbs are a chronological trail of events leading up to an error – navigation, clicks, XHR/fetch calls, console messages, log statements, DB queries. They are buffered in memory and only sent with an event, so they help reproduce what the user or service did before failing. You can add custom ones (Sentry.addBreadcrumb) and filter sensitive ones in beforeBreadcrumb.
Tags vs context vs extra data?

Tags are indexed and searchable key/value strings, used for filtering, grouping in the UI and alert conditions (keep cardinality reasonable). Contexts are structured objects shown on the event (order details, device info) but not indexed. User is a special context to count affected users. Use tags for things you'll filter by, context for detail you'll read.
Why are source maps important and how do you handle them securely?

Minified production JavaScript produces stack traces like main.3f2a.js:1:48213. Uploading source maps for the matching release lets Sentry de-minify traces to the original TypeScript file and line. Generate maps in CI, upload with sentry-cli or the bundler plugin, and remove them from the deployed assets (or use hidden source maps) so your source isn't publicly downloadable.
What are releases and environments used for?

environment separates dev/staging/prod events for filtering and alert routing. release tags events with the deployed version, enabling "first seen in release", regression detection, suspect commits, release health (crash-free sessions) and matching source maps. Set both from CI so they are consistent across back end and front end.
What is sampling and how do you choose rates?

Sampling sends only a fraction of events to control volume and cost. Errors are typically kept at 100%, while transactions are sampled (e.g. 5–20% in production, 100% in dev). Use tracesSampler to drop noise like health checks and keep critical flows at higher rates. Sampling decisions propagate in distributed traces so a trace is either complete or dropped.
How does Sentry group errors, and what if grouping is wrong?

Sentry fingerprints events primarily from in-app stack frames, otherwise from exception type and normalised message, and events with the same fingerprint form one issue. If unrelated errors merge or one error splits into many (e.g. dynamic IDs in messages), set a custom fingerprint in the SDK, add server-side fingerprint/stack-trace rules, or merge issues manually.
What kinds of alerts would you configure?

Issue alerts for new issues and regressions in production, and frequency alerts (e.g. more than 100 events or 50 users in an hour). Metric alerts on error rate, p95 transaction duration or failure rate of key endpoints. Route critical alerts to on-call (PagerDuty/Slack) and the rest to a channel or Jira, with ownership rules assigning issues to teams to avoid alert fatigue.
How do you prevent sensitive data (PII) from reaching Sentry?

Keep sendDefaultPii false, set only a user ID rather than email/name, and never put personal or medical data in exception messages or tags. Scrub fields in beforeSend and beforeBreadcrumb, enable server-side data scrubbing and advanced scrubbing rules, disable IP storage, and keep Session Replay masking on. For strict compliance, choose data residency, shorter retention, or self-hosted Sentry.
Sentry vs Splunk vs an APM tool like Datadog or New Relic?

Sentry is developer-centric error tracking with code-level context, grouping and release tracking plus tracing. Splunk is a log ingestion and search platform used for operations, security (SIEM) and analytics across all log data. APM tools cover performance metrics, infrastructure, service maps and traces at scale. They overlap but complement each other – e.g. Sentry for exceptions, Splunk for logs/audit, Prometheus/Grafana or an APM for metrics.
What are the three pillars of observability?

Logs (detailed discrete events), metrics (aggregated numeric time series for dashboards and alerts), and traces (end-to-end request paths across services as spans). Monitoring tells you that something is wrong; observability lets you ask why by correlating the three. OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard for producing all three.
What is a correlation ID and how do you implement it in Spring Boot?

A unique ID per request, created at the entry point (gateway or first service) or taken from an incoming header, propagated to downstream calls and included in every log line, so you can trace one request across services. Implement with a servlet filter that sets it in the MDC and response header, and forward it in RestClient/WebClient/Feign interceptors and Kafka headers. In Spring Boot 3, Micrometer Tracing does this automatically with W3C traceparent and traceId in MDC.
💡 Also attach the ID as a Sentry tag so a support ticket's request ID leads straight to the error.
How do you capture handled exceptions or messages manually?

Call Sentry.captureException(ex) for caught exceptions you still want visibility on, or Sentry.captureMessage("Payment retry exhausted", SentryLevel.WARNING) for notable conditions without an exception. Use Sentry.withScope (Java) or Sentry.withScope(scope => ...) (JS) to add tags/context only to that event. Don't report expected business validation errors – they create noise.
What are SLI, SLO, SLA and an error budget?

An SLI is a measurement of good events over total events (successful, fast requests). An SLO is the internal target for it, such as 99.9% over 30 days. An SLA is the external contract, usually looser, with consequences if missed. The error budget (100% − SLO) is how much unreliability you can afford; teams use it to balance shipping features against reliability work, and alert on how fast it is being burned.
Your team ignores Sentry because it has thousands of issues. How do you fix it?

- Filter noise at the source: inbound filters, ignoreErrors, denyUrls for extensions, and beforeSend for known harmless errors.
- Fix grouping with fingerprints so one bug is one issue.
- Assign ownership rules so every issue lands with a team.
- Alert only on new issues, regressions and user-impact spikes, routed per team.
- Triage the top issues weekly, resolve them "in next release", and archive the rest with conditions.
💡 The goal is that every alert is actionable.
How does a trace connect the Angular front end with the Spring Boot back end?

The browser SDK starts a transaction for a page load or navigation and attaches sentry-trace and baggage headers to requests whose URLs match tracePropagationTargets. The Java SDK reads these headers and continues the same trace ID, adding spans for the controller, JDBC and outgoing HTTP calls. The backend must allow those headers in CORS. The same idea works with OpenTelemetry's W3C traceparent header.
Breadcrumbs, tags or MDC values go missing for code run in @Async or a thread pool. Why?

Sentry's scope and SLF4J's MDC are stored per thread (thread-local). When work moves to another thread — @Async, CompletableFuture.supplyAsync, an executor — that context is not copied by default. Fix it by wrapping tasks to copy the context: a Spring TaskDecorator that copies MDC.getCopyOfContextMap() and forks the Sentry scope, or Micrometer context-propagation for Reactor. The same caution applies to virtual threads created by a custom executor.
Ad blockers stop Sentry events from the browser. What can you do?

Use the SDK's tunnel option: the browser sends events to an endpoint on your own domain (for example /monitoring), and your backend forwards them to Sentry. Because the request goes to your domain, blockers don't filter it. Validate that the forwarded DSN/project is yours so the endpoint can't be abused as an open proxy, and rate-limit it.
How do you monitor scheduled jobs (for example a nightly @Scheduled task)?

Errors alone don't tell you a job didn't run. Use cron/heartbeat monitoring: the job sends a check-in when it starts and when it finishes (Sentry Cron Monitors, or a heartbeat to an uptime tool), and an alert fires if a check-in is missed or the job runs too long or fails. Also emit a metric for duration and records processed, and log a clear summary line per run.
What does "resolve in next release" do, and what is a regression?

Marking an issue resolved in the next release tells Sentry the fix will ship in the next release it sees (based on the release value set in the SDK and created in CI). Events from older releases don't reopen it, but if the same error happens in the fixed release or later, Sentry reopens it as a regression and can alert. That only works if every deployment sets a correct release (for example the Git SHA or version).
